_doc: Evidence library. One entry per source. 'label' is the evidence-strength label (established | emerging | none); programme records use kind 'programme' and label 'none' (Programme information is not an evidence-strength assessment). 'result' flags the direction: positive | negative | inconclusive | mixed | descriptive | not-conducted | guidance. 'verification' as in facts.json. 'notes' is internal. 'public': false keeps an entry out of the public library.

items.label: established
items.authors: Fusar-Poli P, Borgwardt S, et al.
items.title: The psychosis high-risk state: a comprehensive state-of-the-art review
items.population: People meeting clinical high-risk criteria (review of the field)
items.finding: Describes how the high-risk state is defined and assessed, including attenuated psychotic symptoms and brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms.
items.limitations: A narrative review, not a systematic estimate of outcomes.
items.notes: Genetic-risk-with-deterioration wording not confirmed as a statement in this paper.
items.finding_check: Not confirmed: the card's finding is a paraphrase, not a contiguous passage of the abstract (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.authors: Addington J, Cornblatt BA, Cadenhead KS, et al.
items.title: At clinical high risk for psychosis: outcome for nonconverters
items.population: People at clinical high risk who did not develop psychosis (NAPLS cohort)
items.design: Longitudinal follow-up of a multisite cohort
items.finding: People who did not develop psychosis were a mixed group: some recovered, others kept milder symptoms and difficulties.
items.limitations: One North American cohort; exact remission percentages not quoted here.
items.finding_check: Consistent with abstract conclusions (paraphrase) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.authors: Fusar-Poli P, Bonoldi I, Yung AR, et al.
items.title: Predicting psychosis: meta-analysis of transition outcomes in individuals at high clinical risk
items.population: People at clinical high risk in published cohorts
items.finding: Pooled risk of developing psychosis rose over time: 18% at 6 months, 22% at 1 year, 29% at 2 years and 36% at 3 years.
items.limitations: Earlier literature; transition rates in later studies were lower (see Salazar de Pablo et al. 2021).
items.finding_check: Matches quoted abstract figures (18%, 22%, 29%, 36%) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.authors: Salazar de Pablo G, Radua J, Pereira J, et al.
items.title: Probability of transition to psychosis in individuals at clinical high risk: an updated meta-analysis
items.population: 9,222 people at clinical high risk in 130 studies
items.design: Meta-analysis (a pooled estimate and, separately, Kaplan–Meier cumulative estimates)
items.finding: Pooled estimate: about one in four (25%) developed psychosis within 3 years. Kaplan–Meier cumulative estimates, a separate analysis: 8% at 6 months, 14% at 1 year, 20% at 2 years, 27% at 3 years and 35% at 10 years. Wide variation between studies.
items.limitations: High heterogeneity between services and criteria; individual risk varies. The pooled and Kaplan–Meier results are separate analyses and are not combined into one series. Neither is interchangeable with the older pooled averages of Fusar-Poli et al. 2012.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted primary text (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.title: Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management (CG178)
items.population: Adults considered at increased risk of psychosis
items.finding: Offer individual CBT, with or without family intervention. Do not offer antipsychotic medication to people at increased risk or to reduce the risk of or prevent psychosis.
items.limitations: Applies in England; guidance differs elsewhere.
items.notes: Published 12 February 2014; last updated and last reviewed 4 September 2026 (NICE guidance page, per Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Recommendation numbers not recorded.
items.finding_check: Partly confirmed. 'Offer individual CBT with or without family intervention' matches the quoted recommendation; 'do not offer antipsychotic medication to people considered to be at increased risk' matches the quoted text, but the card's further limb 'or to reduce the risk of or prevent psychosis' is beyond the passage quoted (truncated with an ellipsis). Recommendation numbers 1.2.3.1 and 1.2.3.2 are as cited by Filipp and are not stated in Web Boss's note (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.title: Psychosis and schizophrenia in children and young people: recognition and management (CG155)
items.population: Children and young people considered at increased risk
items.finding: For children and young people considered at increased risk of psychosis, consider individual CBT with or without family intervention (recommendation 1.2.5). Do not offer antipsychotic medication with the aim of decreasing the risk of psychosis (recommendation 1.2.6).
items.limitations: Applies in England; guidance differs elsewhere.
items.notes: Published 23 January 2013; last updated 26 October 2016; last reviewed 19 September 2024 (NICE guidance page, per Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026).
items.finding_check: Matches recommendations 1.2.5 (CBT) and 1.2.6 (antipsychotics 'with the aim of decreasing the risk of psychosis'), both quoted from the NICE recommendations page (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: Epidyolex 100 mg/ml oral solution: Summary of Product Characteristics
items.population: Patients with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome or tuberous sclerosis complex
items.finding: The UK product information lists Epidyolex as an add-on treatment for seizures associated with Lennox–Gastaut or Dravet syndrome, together with clobazam, and for seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis complex, in patients aged 2 years and older. Its side effects include sleepiness and raised liver enzymes (especially with valproate); interacts with clobazam.
items.limitations: Epilepsy populations at higher doses per kg; not evidence about psychosis.
items.notes: Date of revision of the text 8 June 2026; emc page last updated 18 June 2026 (per Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026).
items.finding_check: Indications match quoted SmPC section 4.1; adverse effects and interactions supported by SmPC text. About Epidyolex only; not an authorisation for NWPT-SM32300 (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: Trial of cannabidiol for drug-resistant seizures in the Dravet syndrome
items.population: 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome
items.finding: CBD 20 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures versus placebo. Common side effects included diarrhoea, vomiting, fatigue, fever, sleepiness and abnormal liver tests.
items.limitations: Epilepsy, not psychosis; cited here for safety information.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted abstract results (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: The contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe (EU-GEI): a multicentre case-control study
items.population: 901 people with first-episode psychosis and 1,237 controls, 11 sites
items.finding: Daily cannabis use, and especially daily use of high-potency (high-THC) cannabis, was associated with higher odds of psychotic disorder.
items.limitations: Association, not proof of cause; about THC-rich cannabis, not CBD.
items.finding_check: Consistent with abstract framing; odds ratios not quoted (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.authors: Bhattacharyya S, Morrison PD, Fusar-Poli P, et al.
items.title: Opposite effects of Δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol on human brain function and psychopathology
items.population: 15 healthy men (plus 6 in a pretreatment experiment)
items.finding: THC and CBD had opposite effects on activity in several brain regions; CBD pretreatment prevented THC-induced psychotic symptoms in a small group.
items.limitations: Very small, healthy volunteers, single doses; mechanism, not clinical benefit.
items.finding_check: Consistent with abstract (not quoted) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.authors: McGuire P, Robson P, Cubala WJ, et al.
items.title: Cannabidiol (CBD) as an adjunctive therapy in schizophrenia: a multicenter randomized controlled trial
items.population: 88 adults with schizophrenia already taking antipsychotics
items.finding: Positive psychotic symptoms fell more with CBD than placebo (small difference), and clinicians more often rated patients as improved. Generally well tolerated.
items.limitations: Small, short, add-on treatment in established schizophrenia; not people at clinical high risk.
items.finding_check: Not confirmed: full text needed for the symptom results (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.title: Cannabidiol enhances anandamide signaling and alleviates psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia
items.population: 42 inpatients with acute schizophrenia
items.product: Oral CBD up to 800 mg/day (not NWPT-SM32300)
items.finding: Symptoms improved similarly with CBD and amisulpride; CBD had fewer movement side effects, less weight gain and a smaller prolactin rise.
items.limitations: Small and short; no placebo group, so the size of any CBD effect alone is uncertain.
items.finding_check: Consistent with abstract theme (not quoted) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.authors: Boggs DL, Surti T, et al.
items.title: The effects of cannabidiol (CBD) on cognition and symptoms in outpatients with chronic schizophrenia: a randomized placebo controlled trial
items.population: 36 outpatients with chronic schizophrenia
items.finding: No improvement in cognition or symptoms compared with placebo.
items.limitations: Small; lower dose than some other studies; stable chronic patients.
items.finding_check: Not confirmed: exact null result to be checked in full text (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.title: Effect of cannabidiol on medial temporal, midbrain, and striatal dysfunction in people at clinical high risk of psychosis: a randomized clinical trial
items.population: 33 people at clinical high risk (16 CBD, 17 placebo) and 19 healthy volunteers
items.product: Single oral CBD 600 mg dose (not NWPT-SM32300)
items.finding: During a memory task, brain activity with CBD was intermediate between the placebo group and healthy volunteers in several regions.
items.limitations: Single dose; brain-activity measures, not symptoms or outcomes.
items.finding_check: Consistent with abstract (not quoted) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.title: Effects of short-term cannabidiol treatment on response to social stress in subjects at clinical high risk of developing psychosis
items.population: 32 people at clinical high risk and 26 healthy volunteers
items.product: Oral CBD 600 mg/day for 7 days (not NWPT-SM32300)
items.finding: Anxiety and stress responses to a public-speaking test were intermediate between placebo and healthy volunteers. The cortisol response did not differ significantly from placebo.
items.limitations: One week; laboratory stress test, not clinical outcomes.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted abstract results (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: emerging
items.authors: Bhattacharyya S, Appiah-Kusi E, Wilson R, et al.
items.title: Effects of cannabidiol on symptoms in people at clinical high risk for psychosis
items.population: 33 people at clinical high risk (16 CBD, 17 placebo)
items.product: Oral CBD 600 mg/day for 21 days (not NWPT-SM32300)
items.design: Randomised, placebo-controlled; published as a short research letter
items.finding: After adjusting for starting scores, symptom and distress scores were lower with CBD than placebo; CBD was well tolerated.
items.limitations: Very small, three weeks, short-letter format; not yet confirmed in a larger trial.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted article text (Europe PMC PDF) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: none
items.authors: Bhattacharyya S, Davies C, Carter B, McGuire P, Brammer M, Fusar-Poli P, Broome M, Watson S, Perez J, Yung A
items.title: Cannabidiol as a treatment for patients who are clinically at high risk of developing psychosis: learnings from the CANTOP-RCT
items.population: Planned: about 300 people at clinical high risk across UK sites
items.product: CBD 600 mg/day vs placebo for 6 months (planned; not NWPT-SM32300)
items.finding: The study did not start owing to challenges in securing supply of the study drug.
items.limitations: Not an efficacy finding, and not the NWPharmaTech Phase 2B study. Included because it explains why a larger trial is still missing.
items.notes: Bibliographic metadata only (published March 2025; recommended citation Efficacy Mech Eval 2026;13(7):197-214; DOI; PMID) confirmed from the official NIHR PDF, NCBI E-utilities and Crossref by Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026 (release-032/records/primary-source/P8-CANTOP-WebBoss-2026-09-27.md). 'year' is the journal citation year, not the publication month. Finding reworded on 27 Sep 2026 to the sentence approved by Filipp; supported by the report's Abstract, Study limitations and future work, PDF page 2 (also Ethics statement, p. 12), per Web Boss's inspection (release-032/records/primary-source/P8-CANTOP-finding-support-WebBoss-2026-09-27.md). Not scientific sign-off. Title and named authors (in the documented order) are taken from the same note.
items.finding_check: Supported by report Abstract, Study limitations and future work, PDF page 2 (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: none
items.title: A Phase 1 study to assess the safety and pharmacokinetics of novel cannabidiol (CBD) soft-gel capsule formulation (NW300EMCBD) in healthy subjects
items.population: 14 healthy adult volunteers aged 18 to 55
items.product: NWPT-SM32300 600 mg and 900 mg; Epidyolex comparator
items.design: Randomised, open-label, three-period crossover; single doses
items.finding: Completed December 2025. Results not yet published.
items.limitations: Healthy volunteers, single doses: measures absorption and short-term tolerability, not effectiveness in clinical high risk of psychosis.
items.finding_check: Completion 10 December 2025 and no posted results confirmed (ClinicalTrials.gov API) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.
items.notes: Registry-derived citation fields use the registry spelling 'NW PharmaTech Ltd' (ClinicalTrials.gov leadSponsor; ISRCTN 'NW PharmaTech'), per Filipp 27 Sep 2026. Transcription only; company branding and sponsor roles elsewhere unchanged.

items.label: established
items.authors: Salazar de Pablo G, Woods SW, Drymonitou G, de Diego H, Fusar-Poli P
items.title: Prevalence of individuals at clinical high-risk of psychosis in the general population and clinical samples: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.population: 37,135 people assessed in 35 studies
items.finding: Clinical high-risk states were uncommon in the general population (1.7%) and much more common among young people already seeking help from services (19.2%).
items.limitations: Estimates depend on how and where people were sampled; confidence intervals are wide.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted primary text (PMC) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: Early interventions to prevent psychosis: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.population: 1,246 people at clinical high risk in 11 randomised trials
items.finding: CBT was associated with fewer transitions to psychosis at 12 months (risk ratio 0.54), on moderate-quality evidence. Evidence for other interventions was low quality. The review did not conclude that any specific intervention is proven.
items.limitations: Small trials; evidence quality mostly low to moderate.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted abstract (RR 0.54; not conclusive) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: Lack of evidence to favor specific preventive interventions in psychosis: a network meta-analysis
items.population: Randomised trials in people at clinical high risk
items.finding: No evidence that any one preventive intervention works better than the others.
items.limitations: Few, small trials per intervention.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted abstract (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: Comprehensive versus usual community care for first-episode psychosis: 2-year outcomes from the NIMH RAISE Early Treatment Program
items.population: 404 people with first-episode psychosis at 34 US clinics
items.product: Coordinated specialty care (NAVIGATE), not a medicine
items.finding: People receiving coordinated specialty care stayed in treatment longer and had better quality of life, symptoms and involvement in work or school; benefits were larger when untreated psychosis had been shorter.
items.limitations: People with first-episode psychosis, not clinical high risk; US community clinics.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted abstract (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: Critical aspects affecting cannabidiol oral bioavailability and metabolic elimination, and related clinical implications
items.population: Review of human pharmacokinetic studies
items.finding: Taken by mouth while fasting, only about 6% of a CBD dose is estimated to reach the bloodstream; a high-fat meal increases this about fourfold. Much of each dose is broken down by the liver before reaching the circulation.
items.limitations: Review of other CBD preparations; figures vary between studies.
items.finding_check: Matches quoted text (about 6%; fourfold with high-fat meal) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: established
items.title: A Phase I, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Single Ascending Dose, Multiple Dose, and Food Effect Trial of the Safety, Tolerability and Pharmacokinetics of Highly Purified Cannabidiol in Healthy Subjects
items.population: Healthy adult volunteers
items.finding: Described the safety and tolerability of single and repeated doses of purified CBD in healthy adults, and found that a high-fat meal increased CBD exposure.
items.limitations: Healthy volunteers; a different CBD product. A published correction exists.
items.notes: Exact food-effect fold changes not confirmed.
items.finding_check: Partly: food effect supported; exact fold changes not confirmed (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.finding: Describes the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2, the body’s own signalling molecules that act at them (such as anandamide and 2-AG), and other compounds that act at these receptors.
items.limitations: Receptor vocabulary and pharmacology; not evidence about clinical effects.

items.label: pending
items.title: Information for Health Care Professionals: Cannabis (marihuana, marijuana) and the cannabinoids
items.population: Not applicable
items.design: Health Canada reference for health care professionals (Spring 2018)
items.finding: Describes the components of the endocannabinoid system: the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2, endocannabinoids such as anandamide and 2-AG, and the enzymes that make and break them down.
items.limitations: A 2018 reference, used here only for basic biology; not current clinical, dosing or regulatory guidance.

Date: Spring 2018 (per Filipp; the capture's date line was not included, and the PDF in the pack is an older February 2013 version, not used). items.finding_check: Section 1.0 'The Endocannabinoid System', subsection 'Components of the endocannabinoid system': 'The ECS consists mainly of: the cannabinoid 1 and 2 (CB1 and CB2) receptors; the cannabinoid receptor ligands N-arachidonoylethanolamine ("anandamide") and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG); the endocannabinoid-synthesizing enzymes … and the endocannabinoid-degrading enzymes fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL)'; 'Anandamide and 2-AG are considered the primary endogenous activators of cannabinoid signaling'. Matches the page and glossary wording. Used only for basic biology; the section's disease list and 'entourage effect' discussion are not used. Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: pending
items.title: Cannabidiol inhibits THC-elicited paranoid symptoms and hippocampal-dependent memory impairment
items.population: 48 healthy participants
items.product: Oral CBD or placebo before intravenous THC (experimental challenge)
items.finding: CBD pretreatment reduced selected paranoia and memory outcomes after THC. The difference in the average positive-symptom (PANSS) score was not statistically significant.
items.limitations: Healthy volunteers; route and timing differ from ordinary cannabis use.
items.metadata_check: Primary record: PubMed 23042808 / Europe PMC abstract record (DOI 10.1177/0269881112460109) (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026)
items.finding_check: Abstract level only (subscription full text, not in PMC): n=22 CBD + 26 placebo = 48; oral CBD 600 mg 210 min before IV THC 1.5 mg; paranoia (SSPS) and memory (HVLT-R) outcomes favoured CBD (p<0.05); lower PANSS positive scores 'did not reach statistical significance'. 'Double-blind' removed from the design: not stated in the abstract (Web Boss, 27 Sep 2026). Not scientific sign-off.

items.label: pending
items.title: Does cannabidiol make cannabis safer? A randomised, double-blind, cross-over trial of cannabis with four different CBD:THC ratios
items.population: 46 healthy, infrequent cannabis users

items.population: 18 healthy adults

items.limitations: Small, single doses; participants also took a mix of probe drugs used to measure drug-metabolising enzymes.

items.label: pending
items.title: Does cannabidiol reduce the adverse effects of cannabis in schizophrenia? A randomised, double-blind, cross-over trial
items.population: 30 people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and cannabis use disorder
items.product: Oral CBD or placebo before inhaled (vaporised) cannabis
items.finding: CBD given before cannabis did not reduce its acute effects on memory or psychotic symptoms, and appeared to worsen them.
